routes.reason: GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights names 'Gross–Zagier, Chapters II–IV' among its primary source contracts, and its layers GZ.2 (admissible pairings), GZ.6 (arithmetic generating series and incoherent analytic kernels, with holomorphic projection), GZ.7 (local arithmetic identities and boundary contributions) and GZ.8 ('Specialize to X₀(N)') are written for Yuan–Zhang–Zhang's adelic proof, of which this paper's theorem is the classical case. The paper's own proof is therefore the blueprint source for the X₀(N) instances of those layers: Chapter II's archimedean heights (Legendre functions Q_{s−1}, the Green's functions G_{N,s}, their values at Heegner points and the counts ρ^m) and Chapter III's finite heights (the Eichler-order models R𝔞, the intersection formula, the explicit quaternion algebras) belong to GZ.7; Chapter IV's Rankin kernel θ_𝒜E_s, its Fourier expansion, the functional equations, holomorphic projection and the explicit coefficient formulas (Theorems IV.5.5–5.8, IV.6.9) belong to GZ.6, together with the classical analytic inputs they need (non-holomorphic Eisenstein series of Γ₀(M) with character, K-Bessel and Legendre functions, Poisson summation over ideal lattices, cusps and coset representatives of Γ₀(ND)\Γ₀(N)), which no other layer plans; the coefficient identity ⟨c,T_mc^σ⟩ = u²a_{m,𝒜}, the Hecke-algebra pairing argument and the corollaries on L-values (Chapter V §1) belong to GZ.8 and GZ.3; the Waldspurger–Vignéras square statement to GZ.5. Every planned item of the paper whose layer is in this roadmap is named too, since the paper supplies its classical statement. No new layer is needed: each item is a step of a theorem these layers already own, specialised to X₀(N).

Chapter III quotes Deuring's reduction theory: the endomorphism ring of an elliptic curve over a field is ℤ, an order in an imaginary quadratic field or a maximal order in the quaternion algebra ramified at p and ∞; the reduction of CM curves (good reduction potentially, supersingular exactly at non-split primes); and the structure of End at a non-split prime. It also uses Kronecker's congruence Φ_p(X,Y) ≡ (X^p − Y)(X − Y^p) mod p for the modular polynomial. CM.5 ('Reduction, isogenies and certified computation', with 'Supersingular reduction cannot be treated as ordinary') is the layer that owns reduction of CM elliptic curves, and CM.3 ('Class polynomials and ring class fields') owns the modular-polynomial arithmetic; the paper is a source for these statements, with Deuring 1941 as the primary reference (see prerequisites).

The theta series θ_𝒜(z) = Σ_{𝔞∈𝒜} e^{2πiN(𝔞)z} of an ideal class and its modularity (a weight-one form of level |D| with character ε) are the input of the Rankin kernel. GN.3 plans 'theta-series interfaces' for quadratic forms, and the theta series of a binary form of discriminant D is its first case; no layer states the weight-one level-|D| modularity, so the paper (Chapters I §5 and IV §1) is a source for that layer.

Chapter IV uses the functional equation of L(s,ε) for the odd quadratic character with root number +1, the evaluation of the quadratic Gauss sum with its sign (Σ ε₂(n)e(rn/δ₂) = ε₂(r)κ(D₂)δ₂^{1/2}) and the analytic class number formula L(1,ε) = πh/(u√|D|). AN.1 plans functional equations whose 'Acceptance' requires 'conductor, Gauss sum and parity', and AN.4 plans the analytic class-number formula; Mathlib has the functional equation with an unevaluated root number and only τ² for the Gauss sum. These are sources for those layers.

Proposition III.(1.4), that the model of X₀(N) over ℤ used for the intersection theory is regular at the points that matter, is the regular-model statement R13.5 ('Bad fibres and regular/semistable models') plans in general; the paper gives the case it needs, with Deligne–Rapoport and Katz–Mazur as references.

Conjecture V.(2.3), that the index of the Heegner point is divisible by the order of the rational torsion, and the worked examples N = 11 and N = 65 (with Kramer's 2-Selmer bound) are statements about the Heegner index in BSD, which BSD.5 ('Rational leading-term quotient and Heegner index formula') owns; the paper is a source for its tests.

routes.title: The effective class number problem after Goldfeld, Gross and Zagier
routes.brief: Build the effective solution of Gauss's class number problem for imaginary quadratic fields from Goldfeld's theorem and the Gross–Zagier formula. Final theorems, exactly as Gross–Zagier state them (Invent. Math. 84, Chapter I §§7–8): Proposition (7.4): the elliptic curve E: −139y² = x³ + 10x² − 20x + 8 (conductor 714877 = 37·139²) has ord_{s=1} L(E,s) = rank E(ℚ) = 3; Theorem (8.1): for any ε > 0 there is an effectively computable constant κ(ε) > 0 such that h(D) > κ(ε)(log|D|)^{1−ε}; (8.2) (Oesterlé, simplified): C(t)h(D) ≥ log|D| with C(t) explicit in the number t of prime divisors of D and log C(t) ~ 4√(t/log t); with Mestre's curve y² − y = x³ − 7x + 6 of conductor 5077 (also of analytic rank 3) this holds for D prime to 5077 with C(1) = 55, i.e. h(D) > (1/55) log|D| for D prime; and, with results of Montgomery and Weinberger, the largest |D| with h(D) = 3 is 907. The roadmap must cover Goldfeld's analytic argument (the L-function of E twisted by the characters of Cl_K, its zeros near s = 1 and the lower bound it forces), Oesterlé's explicit form, the certification that the two curves have analytic rank exactly 3 (sign −1, vanishing of L′(E,1) through the Gross–Zagier formula and the triviality of the Heegner point, and a certified nonzero third derivative), genus theory to pass from (8.2) to (8.1), and the final class-number-3 enumeration. It imports the Gross–Zagier formula from GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights (GZ.8), L-functions of elliptic curves, twists and analytic rank from RankZeroOneBSD (BSD.0, BSD.3), modularity of the curves from EllipticCurveModularity, Dirichlet L-functions and the class number formula from AnalyticNumberTheory (AN.1, AN.4), and genus theory from the pinned libraries; it plans none of these again.
routes.reason: Chapter I §8 derives the effective lower bound for class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields from Goldfeld's theorem and the analytic-rank-3 curve of Proposition (7.4), and quotes Oesterlé's explicit version and the class-number-3 consequence. Nothing in the atlas goes in this direction: no stage mentions Goldfeld's method, Oesterlé's bound, or class-number lower bounds (searches of all stage descriptions for 'Goldfeld', 'Oesterlé', 'class number problem' and effective class-number bounds find only a disclaimer in MetaplecticAutomorphicForms:MP.7 and the twist-selection layer BSD.2). It is a self-contained application with a clear endpoint, so it is a new roadmap rather than a layer of the Gross–Zagier roadmap, which it imports.

routes.title: Gross–Zagier formulas and arithmetic heights, Part II: higher weight, Heegner cycles and higher Green's functions
routes.brief: Extend the Gross–Zagier roadmap to weight 2k > 2, following Chapter V §4 of Gross–Zagier. Final statements, exactly as the paper gives them: Theorem (4.1)/(4.2): for k > 1, ε(p) = 1 for all p | N, there is a cusp form Φ = Σ_{m≥1} a_{m,𝒜}q^m ∈ S_{2k}(Γ₀(N)) with L′_𝒜(f,k) = (2^{4k−1}π^{2k}/((2k−2)!√|D|))·(f,Φ) for all f ∈ S^{new}_{2k}(Γ₀(N)), and for m prime to N, a_{m,𝒜} = (m^{k−1}/u²)γ^m_{N,k}(𝒜) + (h/u)r_𝒜(m)m^{k−1}log(N/m) − m^{k−1}Σ_{0<n≤m|D|/N} σ′_𝒜(n)r_𝒜(m|D| − nN)P_{k−1}(1 − 2nN/(m|D|)), where γ^m_{N,k}(𝒜) is a sum of values of the higher Green's function G^m_{N,k} (built from the Legendre function Q_{k−1}) at pairs of Heegner points; Corollary (4.3): for a relation λ (integers λ_m, almost all zero, with Σλ_m a_m = 0 on S_{2k}(Γ₀(N)) and λ_m = 0 for m not prime to N), γ_{N,k,λ}(𝒜) is an explicit rational combination of logarithms of primes, and exp((D^{k−1}/u²)γ_{N,k,λ}(𝒜)) is rational (a square unless |D| is prime); Conjecture (4.4): for such λ there is α ∈ H^× with G_{N,k,λ}(x^τ,x^{στ}) = u²D^{1−k}log|α^τ| for all τ ∈ Gal(H/K). Cover: the higher Green's functions G^m_{N,k} and their Fourier expansions (including the example (4.5) for N = 1, k = 2), relations for S_{2k}(Γ₀(N)), Theorem (4.1) from the weight-2k analysis of Chapter IV (Theorem IV.5.8, imported from GZ.6's source route), Corollary (4.3), the statement of Conjecture (4.4) and its refinement, and the conjectural interpretation of (4.1) as heights of Heegner cycles on Kuga–Sato varieties (Deligne's Heegner vectors). Import the Kuga–Sato varieties, Heegner cycles and Abel–Jacobi maps from GeneralizedHeegnerCycles (GH.0–GH.1), the weight-two theory and normalizations from GrossZagierAndArithmeticHeights (GZ.0, GZ.6–GZ.8) and modular forms of weight 2k from the Tau Ceti ModularForms roadmap; do not replan them. The design job should survey the later literature on Conjecture (4.4) and on heights of Heegner cycles before fixing the endpoint.
routes.reason: Chapter V §4 gives a proved analytic identity in weight 2k > 2 (Theorem 4.1 with Corollary 4.3) and the algebraicity conjecture (4.4) for higher Green's functions at Heegner points. This is the Gross–Zagier formula's direction continued to higher weight, but the parent roadmap has no layer for it: GZ.0–GZ.9 are weight two, and GeneralizedHeegnerCycles (GH.0–GH.8) builds Heegner cycles for p-adic and Kolyvagin-system purposes and does not plan complex heights of Heegner cycles, higher Green's functions or Conjecture (4.4) (stage-description search). So it is new layers in the parent's direction: a Part II.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter II, §1, pp. 235–236 (action of w_d on Heegner points, and (i)), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: p. 235: "The effect of w_d (d‖N) on a Heegner point is to map it to another Heegner point with 𝒜 replaced by 𝒜[𝔡], where 𝔡=(d, 𝔫), and an 𝔫 obtained by making the opposite choice of 𝔭_i for all p_i dividing d."  p. 236: "i) w_N acts on Heegner points by (𝒜, 𝔫)→(𝒜[𝔫], 𝔫̄);"
sourceIssues.correction: 𝒜 is replaced by 𝒜[𝔡]⁻¹ (= 𝒜[𝔡̄]); (i) w_N : (𝒜, 𝔫) → (𝒜[𝔫]⁻¹, 𝔫̄) = (𝒜[𝔫̄], 𝔫̄). This is the rule the paper itself uses on p. 243: τ_{𝒜,𝔫} ↦ τ_{𝒜[𝔡]⁻¹, 𝔫𝔡⁻¹𝔡̄}.
sourceIssues.reason: Chap. I (2.2): w_d(x) = (E/D → E′/D′) with D ⊂ ker φ of order d. For x = (ℂ/𝔞 → ℂ/𝔞𝔫⁻¹): D = 𝔞𝔡⁻¹/𝔞, E/D = ℂ/𝔞𝔡⁻¹ of class 𝒜[𝔡]⁻¹, and the new kernel gives 𝔫𝔡⁻¹𝔡̄. For w_N (dual isogeny, Chap. I (2.1)): ℂ/𝔞𝔫⁻¹ → ℂ/𝔞N⁻¹ = ℂ/(𝔞𝔫⁻¹)𝔫̄⁻¹, i.e. ([𝔞𝔫⁻¹], 𝔫̄). In coordinates: −1/(Nτ) is the root of [CN, −B, A/N], whose (1.5)-ideal is 𝔫̄·(ℤC + ℤ(−B+√D)/2) ~ 𝔞𝔫̄; numerically class(𝔞′) = class(𝔞𝔫̄) ≠ class(𝔞𝔫) for (D, N) = (−23, 2), (−23, 3), (−47, 2), (−71, 2) (SCR/t_wN.py). The rule is independent of the labelling convention of PAPER-GROSS-ZAGIER-86/E3. The p. 243 claim that the substitution fixes 𝒜₁𝒜₂[𝔫]⁻¹ holds only with [𝔡]⁻¹. Reach: p. 243 states and uses the correct rule; statement (ii) is true either way.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter II, §1, (1.3)–(1.5), p. 236, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: "(1.3) β∈ℤ/2Nℤ, β²≡D(mod 4N) ... 𝔫=(N, (β+√D)/2)=ℤN+ℤ(β+√D)/2. The point in 𝔥 corresponding to a Heegner point x=(ℂ/𝔞→ℂ/𝔞𝔫⁻¹) with 𝔞𝔫⁻¹ integral is then the solution τ of a quadratic equation (1.4) Aτ²+Bτ+C=0, A>0, B²−4AC=D, A≡0(mod N), B≡β(mod 2N), with (1.5) 𝔞=ℤ·A+ℤ(B+√D)/2, 𝔞𝔫⁻¹=ℤ·AN⁻¹+ℤ(B+√D)/2, N_{K/ℚ}(𝔞)=A."
sourceIssues.correction: With √D = i√|D| (the branch §3 uses: "τ_i∈A_i⁻¹𝔞̄_i=𝔞_i⁻¹" in (3.7) and "cτ₁+d=(β−α)/(τ₂−τ̄₂)=(A₂/√D)(β−α)" on p. 245) the root τ ∈ 𝔥 represents (ℂ/𝔞̄ → ℂ/𝔞̄𝔫̄⁻¹) = c(x), i.e. the pair (𝒜⁻¹, 𝔫̄); x itself is −τ̄ = (B+√D)/(2A). Consistent fixes: read (β+√D)/2, (B+√D)/2 as (−β+√D)/2, (−B+√D)/2 in (1.3), (1.5) (then (3.7) reads τ_i ∈ 𝔞̄_i⁻¹), or keep (1.3)–(1.5) and read τ_{𝒜,𝔫} in §3 as the Heegner point (𝒜⁻¹, 𝔫̄), on which σ_𝒜 acts by 𝒜₁ ↦ 𝒜₁𝒜.
sourceIssues.reason: §1 dictionary (p. 234): z = ω₁/ω₂ for an oriented basis ⟨ω₁, ω₂⟩ of L with ⟨ω₁, ω₂/N⟩ a basis of L′. For L = 𝔞 = ℤA + ℤ(B+√D)/2 and L′ = 𝔞𝔫⁻¹ = ℤA/N + ℤ(B+√D)/2 this is ω₁ = (B+√D)/2, ω₂ = A (Im(ω₁ω̄₂) = A√|D|/2 > 0), z = (B+√D)/(2A), a root of Az² − Bz + C with B-invariant −β (mod 2N), which differs from β for N > 1 because (β, N) = 1; equivalently Aτ = (−B+√D)/2 ∈ 𝔞̄, so ⟨τ, 1⟩ ~ 𝔞̄ (checked numerically for D = −7, −23: Aτ ∈ 𝔞̄, Aτ ∉ 𝔞). The paper states that 'this invariant corresponds to the choice of 𝔫 as in (1.3)'; under the dictionary it corresponds to 𝔫̄. Reach: : every result of Chapter II depends on the classes only through r_𝒜, r_𝔅, δ(n), the genera {𝒜}, {𝔅𝔫}, all invariant under (𝒜, 𝔅, 𝔫) ↦ (𝒜⁻¹, 𝔅⁻¹, 𝔫̄); (3.14)/(3.17) were verified numerically in the τ-labelling. Chunks reading §4–§5 and Chapter V (individual terms (3.1), χ-components) should keep the labelling in mind: it swaps χ and χ⁻¹, which the paper's final formulas pair symmetrically..

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter II, §3, (3.11) Proposition and the converse step on p. 245, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: "(3.11) Proposition. Let 𝒜₁, 𝒜₂ be two ideal classes of K, 𝔫 a primitive ideal of norm N and 𝔞_i (i=1, 2) an integral ideal in 𝒜_i with 𝔫|𝔞_i, N(𝔞_i)=A_i. Then for m∈ℕ, r_{𝒜₁𝒜₂⁻¹}(m)=0 we have: ... ρ^m(n) = #{(α, β)∈(𝔞₁⁻¹𝔞̄₂⁻¹×𝔞₁⁻¹𝔞₂⁻¹𝔫)/{±1} | N(α)=(Nn+m|D|)/(A₁A₂), N(β)=Nn/(A₁A₂), A₁A₂α≡A₁A₂β(mod 𝔡)}"; p. 245: "If α and β satisfy (3.7) and (3.10) then the right-hand sides of these two equations are in 𝔫𝔞₁⁻¹=Nℤτ₁+ℤ and 𝔞₁⁻¹=ℤτ₁+ℤ, respectively"
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis that 𝔞₁, 𝔞₂ are prime to D (possible in every class, keeping 𝔫 | 𝔞_i), or replace (3.10) by the exact conditions (A₂/√D)(β − α) ∈ 𝔫𝔞₁⁻¹ and (A₂/√D)(τ̄₂β − τ₂α) ∈ 𝔞₁⁻¹.
sourceIssues.reason: The converse divides by √D; at a ramified 𝔭 | 𝔞₁ (or 𝔞₂) the numbers A₁A₂α, A₁A₂β lie in 𝔭 automatically, so (3.10) carries no information there. Counterexample (SCR/t_rho.py, t_rho2.py): D = −7, N = 2, β = 1, m = 3 (3 inert, h = 1), τ₂ from [2, 1, 1], 𝔞₁ = ℤ14 + ℤ(21+√−7)/2 from [14, 21, 8] (N(𝔞₁) = 14, 𝔞₁ ⊂ (√−7)): the true γ-counts are ρ(1), ρ(2), ρ(4), ρ(8) = 2, 2, 6, 8 while the (α, β)-set of (3.11) has 4, 4, 12, 16 elements (every n with 7 ∤ n doubles; n = 14, 28 agree); with 𝔞₁ from [2, 1, 1] (prime to 7) the two counts agree for all n ≤ 29. The p. 246 argument for (3.13) ('exactly half of the pairs') also presupposes 𝔞_i prime to D. Reach: Proposition (3.11) in its stated generality); nothing downstream: (3.12)–(3.17) are statements about classes and follow with representatives prime to D (verified numerically.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter II, §5, normalization of the uniformizing parameter g at an elliptic point, p. 250 (display after 'In general, ω has order 1/u − 1 at x'), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)

sourceIssues.correction: ω = (1/u)(g^{1/u} + higher degree terms) dg/g, i.e. ω = d(g^{1/u})·(1 + …); equivalently, keep the printed display with g replaced by u^u·g.
sourceIssues.reason: At a Heegner point x with u > 1 the local parameter of X₀(N) is (w − z)^u·(unit), and ω = 2πiη⁴(w) dw. With the printed normalization one gets g = (2πiη⁴(z)(w − z)/u)^u(1 + o(1)), so log|g(y)|_v − u log|2πiη⁴(z)(w − z)|_v → −u log|u|_v ≠ 0, contradicting (5.5) (p. 251), which is what (5.6)–(5.8) use. With the corrected normalization g = (2πiη⁴(z)(w − z))^u(1 + o(1)) and (5.5) holds. Independent check against the non-archimedean normalization Ch. III (8.3) (p. 263, N = 1): from ω^{⊗6} = Δ(dq/q)^{⊗6} and q dj/dq = −E₆j/E₄ one gets ω = dj/(j^{2/3}(j − 1728)^{1/2}) up to a root of unity; at j = 1728 (u = 2) the corrected normalization gives ∂/∂t = 2⁶·3⁴ ∂/∂j and the printed one 2⁸·3⁴ ∂/∂j, and at j = 0 (u = 3) the corrected one gives |2⁹·3^{3/2}| and the printed one |2⁹·3^{9/2}|; (8.3), read on a full-resolution IIIF crop of image 00000269, prints 'α ≡ j(x)^{2/3}(j(x) − 1728)^{1/2} (mod μ₀), j(x) ≠ 0, 1728; ≡ 2⁶ · 3⁴, j(x) = 1728; ≡ 2⁹ · 3^{3/2}, j(x) = 0' — exactly the three values computed with the corrected normalization (the generic value j^{2/3}(j − 1728)^{1/2} is the same for both, since u = 1 there). So (5.5), (5.6)–(5.8) and (8.3) are mutually consistent and only the display on p. 250 is off. Under the paper's standing assumption that D is odd this concerns only D = −3 (u = 3) with r_A(m) ≠ 0. The display on p. 250 was re-checked on imgHR/p250.jpg and a zoomed IIIF crop of image 00000256: it reads 'ω = (g^{1/u} + higher degree terms) dg/g'. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (Conrad 2004, §9, conrad.txt pp. 34–38 and 42: the factor u_x^k in (9.4), (9.8) and Theorem 9.2, and the archimedean uniformizer g_{z_v}(z′) = 2πiη⁴(z_v)(z′ − z_v) of Theorem 9.6, which Conrad says is 'exactly the archimedean height contribution which is computed in [GZ, Ch II, (5.3), (5.5)]'; Conrad also says the GZ tangent-vector method is recovered only 'if one avoids the quadratic fields K = Q(√−1) and K = Q(√−3)', but does not name this misprint).)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter III, §1, definition of 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} (p. 254) and the description of the cusps (p. 255), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: Let 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} be the algebraic stack classifying cyclic isogenies of degree N between generalized elliptic curves over S (1.1) φ: E → E′ such that the group scheme A = ker φ meets every irreducible component of each geometric fibre. … Let X be the coarse moduli scheme associated to the stack 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} … The component Cusp(d) corresponds to diagrams of Néron polygons where A = ker φ is isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ.
sourceIssues.correction: For N squarefree this is the Deligne–Rapoport description. For general N the model should be taken as the normalization model of X₀(N) over ℤ (Deligne–Rapoport, Katz–Mazur ch. 8), or as the coarse space of Česnavičius' refined stack (which adds, for every d | N, an ample cyclic subgroup of order d); and at Cusp(d) the kernel A is a cyclic group scheme that is an extension of dℤ/Nℤ ≅ ℤ/(N/d)ℤ by μ_d, isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ only when gcd(d, N/d) = 1.
sourceIssues.reason: (i) Check: Cusp(d) ≅ Spec ℤ[μ_f] is flat over ℤ, so its geometric points include characteristic-0 points; there μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ ≅ ℤ/d × ℤ/(N/d) is not cyclic when f = gcd(d, N/d) > 1, contradicting the cyclicity condition (1.2) that defines 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)}. On a Néron polygon a cyclic A of order N meeting every component is e.g. ⟨(ζ_N, 1)⟩ ⊂ G_m × ℤ/(N/d), a non-split extension. (ii) Česnavičius, 'A modular description of X₀(n)', Algebra & Number Theory 11 (2017) (arXiv:1511.07475), abstract: 'when a positive integer n is not squarefree, even over ℂ the moduli stack that parametrizes generalized elliptic curves equipped with an ample cyclic subgroup of order n does not agree at the cusps with the Γ₀(n)-level modular stack'. The stack of (1.1)–(1.2) is exactly that naive stack. Katz–Mazur [21] treat [Γ₀(N)] only for elliptic curves and compactify by normalization, so the generalized-elliptic-curve description is not in the cited sources for non-squarefree N. Wording re-checked on imgHR/p254.jpg and p255.jpg ('A = ker φ is isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ'). (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Česnavičius 2017 (for the moduli description at the cusps); the inconsistency with the stated group structure μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ is new. The atlas stage ModularCurvesPartII:R13.2 already routes around it ('Follow Česnavičius' refined description when the naive cyclic-subgroup formulation fails')..)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter III, §2, paragraph after (2.1), p. 256, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: Using the fact that k is algebraically closed, one can check that the definition of Hom_S(y, x) is independent of the diagrams chosen to represent the points x and y.
sourceIssues.correction: True for S = W (a complete DVR of characteristic 0 with algebraically closed residue field: two W-diagrams inducing the same W-point are isomorphic, Conrad Theorem 2.6) and hence for the reductions to W/πⁿ of fixed W-diagrams, which is the only way §§4–9 use it; false for general complete local S (e.g. artinian S) at points with Aut_k ≠ ⟨±1⟩, where Hom_S must be defined for chosen diagrams.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample: p ≥ 5, N = 2, E: y² = x³ − x over 𝔽̄_p with p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (ordinary, j = 1728), A = ⟨(0,0)⟩, which is stable under [i]: (x, y) ↦ (−x, iy); so Aut_k(x₀) = μ₄. The universal deformation ring is W[[T]] with Aut/±1 = ℤ/2 acting faithfully (Conrad p. 12), linearizably T ↦ −T, so the complete local ring of X is W[[T²]] (Conrad Lemma 4.2). Over S = k[ε]/(ε²) the deformations T ↦ 0 (constant) and T ↦ ε both give T² ↦ 0, i.e. the same S-point of X, but they are not isomorphic: the constant one has Aut_S = μ₄, while [i] carries T ↦ ε to T ↦ −ε ≠ ε, so the other has Aut_S = ±1. Hence Card Hom_S(y, y)_{deg 1} is 4 or 2 depending on the representing diagram. Wording re-checked on imgHR/p256.jpg. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (Conrad 2004 restricts to W-diagrams: Theorem 2.6 and Lemma 4.2, conrad.txt pp. 6 and 11).)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter III, §8, convention (8.1), p. 263, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: (8.1)  (x · x) = ord_v(α)  where α∂/∂t is a basis for the free W-module T_x X.
sourceIssues.correction: (x · x) = ord_v(α), where ∂/∂t = α·(a basis of T_x X); equivalently α^{-1}∂/∂t is a basis of T_x X, or αω_x is a basis of the cotangent line when ω_x is the covector dual to ∂/∂t. This is Conrad's α_x.
sourceIssues.reason: (i) Derivation. Take f with ord_x f = 1, write f = T·h with T the integral local parameter of the section x, and normalise g by dg(∂/∂t) = 1. The local symbol of Ch. II (5.1)/(5.3) gives ⟨x, div f⟩_v = log|(f/g)(x)|_v. If ∂/∂t = c·∂/∂T, then (T/g)(x) = c, so the self-intersection that makes (0.2) hold is ord_v(c), with c defined by ∂/∂t = c·basis. (ii) Consistency. With that reading, (8.2) (ord_v α = ½Σ(#Aut_{W/π^n} − #Aut_W) ≥ 0) and (8.3) (α ≡ j^{2/3}(j−1728)^{1/2}, read on the high-resolution scan) are correct. For N = 1 one computes ω = η⁴dq/q = −j^{−2/3}(j−1728)^{−1/2} dj, so ∂/∂t = −j^{2/3}(j−1728)^{1/2}∂/∂j. Under the printed wording, α would be the reciprocal j^{−2/3}(j−1728)^{−1/2}, with ord_v(α) ≤ 0, contradicting (8.2) and (8.3). Conrad's Theorem 8.4 defines (x.x) = ord_v(α_x) with α_xω_x a basis of Cot_x, and his (9.9) and Definition 9.5 show that this equals GZ's ½Σ(#Aut_{W/π^n} − #Aut_W) when v ∤ N. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Conrad 2004, Remark 8.5 ('Our α_x is the reciprocal of the α in [GZ]').)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter III, §8, sentence before Proposition (8.6), p. 264, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: Using the action of w_N on ω, one can show that the tangent vector ∂/∂t spans the submodule (N)^u T_x X when v|n̄.
sourceIssues.correction: ∂/∂t spans (N)^{−u} T_x X when v|n̄, i.e. ∂/∂t = N^{−u}·(generator). Equivalently ω_x is N^u times a generator of the cotangent line. With the corrected (8.1) (see PAPER-GROSS-ZAGIER-86/E16) this gives (x·x) = −u·ord_v(N), and hence Proposition (8.6) as printed.
sourceIssues.reason: When v|n̄ the kernel of φ is étale at p, and x lies on the fibral component through the cusp 0 = Cusp(1) (Prop. 3.1). Near that cusp the integral parameter is q′ = e^{2πiτ′}, τ′ = −1/(Nτ), attached to the Tate curve Tate(q′^N) with subgroup ⟨q′⟩. From η(−1/(Nτ′)) = (Nτ′/i)^{1/2}η(Nτ′) one gets ω = 2πiη⁴(τ)dτ = −N·η⁴(q′^N)dq′/q′. So ω vanishes to order ord_p(N) along that component: it is N times a generator. Equivalently, on the étale-kernel component the forgetful map (E→E′) ↦ E is inseparable (Frobenius), so ω = π_1^*ω_1 ≡ 0 mod p. The dual vector ∂/∂t is therefore N^{−1}·(generator) when u = 1; for u > 1 the normalisation ω = (g^{1/u}+…)dg/g raises this to N^{−u}. Conrad's Lemma 10.1 independently gives ord_{v,x}(Δ) = 6u·ord_v(N) in exactly this étale case, i.e. Δ(dq/q)^{⊗6} = ω^6 is N^6 times a generator. The printed (8.6) value −u r_𝒜(m) ord_p(N) is correct (Conrad Thm 10.4). It is obtained from the printed '(N)^u' only together with the literal (inverted) wording of (8.1), so the two misstatements cancel. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (the underlying fact is Conrad 2004, Lemma 10.1 and Theorem 10.4, which do not comment on GZ's sentence).)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter III, §9, choice of the auxiliary prime q and the order S, p. 265 (inert case), and the ramified analogue (9.8), p. 266, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: Fix an auxiliary prime q with (q/l) = (−p/l) for all primes l|D. ... S = {α+βj: α∈𝔡^{-1}, β∈𝔡^{-1}𝔮^{-1}𝔫, α≡β mod O_𝔣}  [ramified case: 'q ... with (q/p′) = (−1/p′) for all p′≠p which divide D and (−q/p) = −1']
sourceIssues.correction: For S (with the congruence α ≡ β) to be an order one needs −pq ≡ 1 (mod l) for every prime l|D, i.e. −pq ≡ 1 (mod D); in the ramified case one needs −q ≡ 1 (mod D/p). Both can be imposed alongside GZ's conditions and still met by Dirichlet's theorem. Alternatively use the congruence α ≡ Xβ with N(X) ≡ −pq (mod D) (Mann's S_X, (A.5)/(A.6)). The sign bookkeeping α ≡ ±β in (9.3), (9.8) and in the proof of (9.7) then applies verbatim.
sourceIssues.reason: Let l|D and let 𝔣 be the prime over l. Take α = β ∈ 𝔡^{-1} with a simple pole at 𝔣; then α+βj ∈ S. Its reduced norm is N(α)+pqN(β) = (1+pq)N(β), and ord_l N(β) = −1. So the norm is l-integral only if l | 1+pq. GZ's condition says only that −pq is a square mod l (e.g. −pq ≡ 4 mod l is allowed), so S can contain elements of non-integral reduced norm, and is then not an order. The proof of (9.7) also uses −pq ≡ 1 mod l when it concludes that integrality of mN𝔞 = Nα + pqNβ forces α ≡ ±β mod O_𝔣. With −pq ≡ X² one gets only α ≡ ±Xβ. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Mann, appendix to Conrad 2004, p. 57 ('certainly one does not get an order in (A.5) using X = 1 unless −pq ≡ 1 mod D'; ramified case: 'take X = 1 (as in [GZ]) by also requiring −q ≡ 1 mod D/p'), and Remark A.7.)

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter V, §2, p. 310, definition of P_K, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: belongs to E(K). Up to sign, it is independent of the choice of the Heegner point x
sourceIssues.correction: Up to sign and the addition of a rational torsion point, P_K is independent of the choice of x
sourceIssues.reason: The 2^s·h Heegner points of discriminant D are permuted simply transitively by W × Gal(H/K) (Chap. II, p. 239; Chap. I, p. 227), so another choice is x' = w_Q(x^τ). Since w_Q acts on the f-part by the eigenvalue λ_Q = ±1, π∘w_Q − λ_Q π is a morphism X₀(N) → E pulling back ω to 0, hence constant, equal to π(w_Q(∞)): the image of a rational cusp, a torsion point of E(ℚ) by Manin–Drinfeld. So P'_K = λ_Q P_K + h·π(w_Q(∞)). This differs from ±P_K whenever P_K has infinite order and h·π(w_Q(∞)) ≠ 0. For instance N = 11, E = X₀(11), π(0) = (0) − (∞) has order 5, and any K with h_K prime to 5 and P_K non-torsion gives such a case. Heights, ranks and all conclusions of §2 are insensitive to torsion.

sourceIssues.locator: Chapter V, §1, proof of Theorem (6.3) of Chap. I, p. 308, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
sourceIssues.printed: Extend {f} to a basis f_1=f, f_2, …, f_d of S_2(Γ_0(N)) consisting of the normalized newforms together with a basis of the space of oldforms … c_χ can be written as a sum of components transforming like the f_j, say c_χ = Σ_{j=1}^d c_χ^{(j)} with T_m c_χ^{(j)} = a_m(f_j) c_χ^{(j)}
sourceIssues.correction: Decompose only along f: by multiplicity one there is an idempotent e_f ∈ 𝕋⊗ℂ projecting onto the f-isotypical part. Write c_χ = e_f c_χ + (1 − e_f)c_χ with T_m e_f c_χ = a_m(f) e_f c_χ for all m; the two parts are orthogonal for <,> (T_m, (m,N) = 1, self-adjoint with different eigencharacters). The generating series of the second part is a form orthogonal to f, so (Σχ(𝒜)g_𝒜, f) = h^{−1}ĥ(c_{χ,f})(f,f) as claimed.
sourceIssues.reason: For an arbitrary basis of the oldspace, 'a_m(f_j)' is not an eigenvalue, and the old part of 𝕋⊗ℂ need not be semisimple (e.g. U_p on oldforms when p² | N), so the stated decomposition with T_m c^{(j)} = a_m(f_j)c^{(j)} for all m cannot hold in general. Only the f-component is used, so the conclusion stands.
